difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY - one concept (the definition of entailment and its equivalent implication and refutation forms). Each statement is a direct restatement or the converse, so no option needs separate non-trivial work; about 45 seconds.
stem:
Sentence $X$ is said to entail Sentence $Y$ if whenever $X$ is $\mathit{TRUE}$, $Y$ also must hold $\mathit{TRUE}$.

Which of the following statements is/are correct if $X$ entails $Y$?

solution.quick:
$X \models Y$ means that every model (truth assignment) making $X$ true also makes $Y$ true. So the only row that falsifies $X \Rightarrow Y$ ($X$ true, $Y$ false) never occurs. That makes $X \Rightarrow Y$, read in words as "if $X$ then $Y$", true in every model: (A) and (C). Equivalently, $X \land \neg Y$ is FALSE in every model: (B).

The converse "if $Y$ then $X$" need not hold, so (D) is wrong. **(A), (B), (C)**

steps.title: Entailment in terms of models
steps.body:
A *model* is an assignment of truth values under which a sentence can be evaluated. Write $M(S)$ for the set of models in which sentence $S$ is TRUE. The definition in the question says

$$
X \models Y \iff \text{in every model where } X \text{ is TRUE, } Y \text{ is TRUE} \iff M(X) \subseteq M(Y).
$$

So entailment rules out exactly one combination: a model in which $X$ is TRUE and $Y$ is FALSE.

steps.title: Truth table with the forbidden row removed
steps.body:
| $X$ | $Y$ | $X \Rightarrow Y$ | $X \land \neg Y$ | $Y \Rightarrow X$ | Possible when $X \models Y$? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T | T | T | F | T | yes |
| T | F | F | T | T | **no (ruled out)** |
| F | T | T | F | **F** | yes |
| F | F | T | F | T | yes |

Look only at the rows that can occur (rows 1, 3 and 4):

- $X \Rightarrow Y$ is T in all of them, so it holds in every model (it is *valid*).
- $X \land \neg Y$ is F in all of them, so it is FALSE in every model (it is *unsatisfiable*).
- $Y \Rightarrow X$ is F in row 3, which entailment does not exclude.

steps.title: Options (A) and (C): the implication holds
steps.body:
From the table, $X \Rightarrow Y$ is TRUE in every model. This is the **deduction theorem**:

$$
X \models Y \iff \models (X \Rightarrow Y).
$$

Option (C), "if $X$ then $Y$", is the English reading of the same implication $X \Rightarrow Y$. Both (A) and (C) are **correct**.

steps.title: Option (B): the refutation form
steps.body:
$X \land \neg Y$ is TRUE exactly when $X$ is TRUE and $Y$ is FALSE, which is the combination that entailment forbids. So $X \land \neg Y$ is FALSE in every model (unsatisfiable). Indeed $X \land \neg Y \equiv \neg(X \Rightarrow Y)$, the negation of a valid sentence.

$$
X \models Y \iff X \land \neg Y \text{ is unsatisfiable.}
$$

This is the principle behind proof by contradiction and resolution refutation. Option (B) is **correct**.

steps.title: Option (D): the converse fails
steps.body:
Counterexample: take atoms $P, Q$ with $X = P \land Q$ and $Y = P$.

- Whenever $P \land Q$ is TRUE, $P$ is TRUE, so $X \models Y$.
- In the model $P = \text{T},\ Q = \text{F}$, $Y = P$ is TRUE but $X = P \land Q$ is FALSE. So "if $Y$ then $X$" fails.

Entailment is one-directional. If it held both ways, $X$ and $Y$ would be logically equivalent. Option (D) is **incorrect**.

**Answer: (A), (B), (C).**

solution.teaching:
**Models and entailment.** In propositional logic, a sentence is built from atoms (such as $P$, $Q$) using connectives $\neg, \land, \lor, \Rightarrow, \Leftrightarrow$. A *model* fixes a truth value for each atom, and the sentence then evaluates to TRUE or FALSE. Entailment, $X \models Y$, is a **relation between sentences**. It says that $Y$ is TRUE in every model in which $X$ is TRUE, i.e. the models of $X$ form a subset of the models of $Y$. Think of $X$ as the stronger claim and $Y$ as the weaker claim that follows from it.

**Implication is a connective inside one sentence.** $X \Rightarrow Y$ is a single sentence. It is FALSE in exactly one situation ($X$ TRUE, $Y$ FALSE) and TRUE otherwise. The two ideas are linked by the **deduction theorem**: $X \models Y$ holds exactly when the sentence $X \Rightarrow Y$ is *valid* (TRUE in every model). In words, it reads "if $X$ then $Y$".

**Refutation.** Since $\neg(X \Rightarrow Y) \equiv X \land \neg Y$, the statement "$X \Rightarrow Y$ is valid" is the same as "$X \land \neg Y$ is unsatisfiable". This is how resolution theorem provers and SAT-based checkers test entailment: add the negated goal $\neg Y$ to the knowledge base $X$ and derive a contradiction.

So there are three equivalent ways to say the same thing:

$$
X \models Y \iff \models (X \Rightarrow Y) \iff X \land \neg Y \text{ is unsatisfiable.}
$$

**The converse is a different claim.** $Y \models X$ would say the models of $Y$ lie inside the models of $X$. Together with $X \models Y$, that would make $X$ and $Y$ logically equivalent. Inferring $X$ from $Y$ and $X \Rightarrow Y$ is the fallacy of *affirming the consequent*. For example, "it is raining and cold" entails "it is raining", but "it is raining" does not entail "it is raining and cold".

**Back to this question.** (A) and (C) are the implication form, (B) is the refutation form, and (D) is the converse. So (A), (B) and (C) are correct.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Entailment excludes the only row in which $X \Rightarrow Y$ is FALSE ($X$ TRUE, $Y$ FALSE). So $X \Rightarrow Y$ holds in every model, as the deduction theorem states.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $X \land \neg Y$ would need a model with $X$ TRUE and $Y$ FALSE, and entailment says no such model exists. So $X \land \neg Y$ is FALSE (unsatisfiable). This is the refutation form of entailment.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: "If $X$ then $Y$" is the English reading of $X \Rightarrow Y$, which holds whenever $X \models Y$. It is the definition in the stem restated.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: This is the converse. With $X = P \land Q$ and $Y = P$ we have $X \models Y$, but in the model $P = \text{T}, Q = \text{F}$, $Y$ is TRUE while $X$ is FALSE. So "if $Y$ then $X$" does not follow.

solution.shortcut: Remember the chain $X \models Y \iff \models (X \Rightarrow Y) \iff (X \land \neg Y)$ unsatisfiable. Options (A), (B) and (C) are three phrasings of this one fact, and (D) is the converse, which never follows automatically.
solution.commonTrap: Treating entailment as equivalence and ticking (D). This is the "affirming the consequent" error: $Y$ being TRUE says nothing about $X$. A second slip is rejecting (B) because "$X \land \neg Y$ could be TRUE in some model". Entailment rules out precisely the models where $X$ is TRUE and $Y$ is FALSE, so no such model exists.

answerVerification.checkCode:
from itertools import product
# X, Y range over ALL Boolean functions of 2 atoms (16 each); models = 4 assignments
M = list(product([0, 1], repeat=2))
F = list(product([0, 1], repeat=4))          # truth table of a sentence over the 4 models
ent = lambda X, Y: all(Y[i] for i in range(4) if X[i])
imp = lambda a, b: (not a) or b
ok = dict(A=True, B=True, C=True, D=True); pairs = 0
for X, Y in product(F, F):
    if not ent(X, Y): continue
    pairs += 1
    ok['A'] &= all(imp(X[i], Y[i]) for i in range(4))        # X => Y valid
    ok['B'] &= not any(X[i] and not Y[i] for i in range(4))  # X & ~Y unsatisfiable
    ok['C'] &= all(imp(X[i], Y[i]) for i in range(4))        # "if X then Y"
    ok['D'] &= all(imp(Y[i], X[i]) for i in range(4))        # converse
print(pairs, 'entailing pairs;', ok); assert ok == dict(A=True, B=True, C=True, D=False)  # -> A;B;C
# explicit counterexample for D: X = P & Q, Y = P, model P=1, Q=0
P, Q = 1, 0; print('X=P&Q:', P and Q, ' Y=P:', P)
answerVerification.notes: X entails Y means M(X) ⊆ M(Y), which rules out only the assignment X=T, Y=F. So X ⇒ Y is valid (deduction theorem), which covers A and C (C is the English reading of the same implication). X ∧ ¬Y is unsatisfiable, which covers B. The converse Y ⇒ X can fail (counterexample X = P ∧ Q, Y = P), so D is false. An exhaustive check over all 16 × 16 pairs of Boolean functions of two atoms (81 entailing pairs) confirms A, B and C always hold and D does not. This matches official key A;B;C.
